title: How an Object Starts: Constructors, the Initialiser List, and the Word explicit

questions.question: What is the difference between setting a member in the constructor's initialiser list and assigning it in the constructor's body?
options: None, they compile to the same thing in every case
In the list the member is built once with its value; in the body it is first built blank and then overwritten, so the work is done twice
The list is only for const members
The body runs first, then the list
questions.explanation: By the time the body runs every member already exists. Measured with a type that counts its own construction: the list built 0 blank and 2 copies with 0 overwrites; the body built 2 blank, 0 copies and overwrote 2.

questions.question: A class lists its members second_, first_ in the constructor's list, but declares first_ before second_. Which is built first?
options: second_, since it is listed first
first_, since members are built in the order they are declared, and gcc and clang warn that the list says otherwise
Whichever is cheaper to build
It is undefined
questions.explanation: Measured: first then second, whatever the list said. The -Wreorder warning is right, because the list is lying about what happens, and it matters when one member's initialiser uses another.

questions.question: A function takes a Loose, a class with a constructor from a double that is not explicit. It is called with the bare number 7. What happens?
options: It does not compile, since 7 is not a Loose
It compiles, and the 7 is silently turned into a Loose
It compiles with a warning on every compiler
It compiles only with a cast
questions.explanation: A constructor callable with one value is also an implicit conversion from that value's type. Marked explicit, the same call is refused by both compilers, and so is the copy form Meters m = 5.0.

questions.question: A class declares only explicit Meters(double). What does the line Meters m; do?
options: Makes a Meters holding zero
Makes a Meters holding whatever was in memory
Does not compile, since declaring any constructor removes the default one
Compiles, and m is unusable until assigned
questions.explanation: gcc: no matching function for call to Meters::Meters(). clang: no matching constructor for initialization. That is the design when a distance with no value would be a lie that looks like a reading.

questions.question: When is it right to write Ramp() = default; for a class that also has other constructors?
options: Always, so the class can be used in containers
When 'has not been given a value' is a state that makes sense, and every member has a default where it is declared
Never, since = default leaves members uninitialised
Only for classes with no members
questions.explanation: = default asks for the constructor the compiler withdrew. It is only worth asking for when the blank state is meaningful, such as a ramp that is not going anywhere, and default member initialisers keep it from leaving members unset, which is lesson 02-09.

questions.question: Why is std::vector<int> v = 5; refused by the compiler?
options: Because 5 is too small a size
Because vector's constructor taking a size is explicit, and 'a vector equal to 5' is not something anybody means
Because int vectors cannot be copy initialised
Because the standard forbids = for containers
questions.explanation: The standard library marks that constructor explicit on purpose. std::vector<int> v(5) says what is meant, and the = form, which would read as 'a vector equal to 5', does not compile.
